title: Aerospace stocks: how to analyze the aircraft industry
description: Aerospace stocks: the order book as buffer, customer prepayments as funding and the engines' moat — how to analyze the aircraft industry with examples.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Aerospace stocks are shares in companies that build aircraft — not the ones that fly them. The distinction is step one of the analysis: an airline sells transport, swinging with fuel prices, load factors and the business cycle; the aircraft industry sells planes and engines to all airlines at once. AK1A's universe carries two companies covering both halves of this supply chain: Airbus the airframe, GE Aerospace the engines. Between them lies the sector's analytical craft — the order book as earnings buffer, prepayments as funding, the aftermarket's moat.

This guide walks the mechanisms with the universe's numbers: delivery series, margins, multiples. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are aerospace stocks — the two supply-chain halves

The market for large passenger aircraft is a duopoly: Airbus and Boeing in principle share the world market, and have since the late 1990s. The barrier is structural — a new aircraft program demands design, tooling, test flights and authority certification over many years and multi-billion sums before first delivery — so nobody steps in and competes on price. Certification sets the tempo: new aircraft arrive when authorities approve them, not when the market wishes.

The engines are an industry inside the industry. GE Aerospace — partly through the CFM partnership with Safran — supplies jet engines to both Airbus and Boeing aircraft: the engines compete even where the airframe half is a duopoly. The universe's numbers show it in one comparison: Airbus reports gross margin 16.3 percent and EBIT margin 8.7, GE Aerospace 31.1 and 20.6 respectively. The gap between 16 and 31 percent gross margin is selling an aircraft once versus selling decades of service on an engine — the mechanics this guide returns to.

## The order book — the earnings buffer visible in advance

An aircraft is sold years before delivery. Contracts are signed, the order book grows, and revenue is recognized only at handover. The consequence is the sector's most valuable property: the order book is an earnings buffer visible in advance. Example: an order book of 8,000 aircraft at 800 deliveries per year gives 8,000 ÷ 800 = ten years of production sold in advance. Compare retail: next quarter's revenue is in practice a forecast — here it stands in contracts. Revenue stability becomes measurable as few industries match, which [revenue stability analysis](/kurser/v12-intaktsstabilitet) captures methodically.

Three caveats keep the picture honest. First: the order book is booked contracts, not cash — deliveries can slip, and during the 2020 pandemic slipped at scale when airlines could not take aircraft. Second: contract prices are set years before delivery — when cost inflation outruns prices, the margin is eaten despite a full order book. Airbus shows that in 2023: revenue grew 11.4 percent (58.8 to 65.4 billion euro) while profit fell 10.8 percent (4,247 to 3,789 M€) — cost inflation and losses in the space program explain the fall. Third: the same leverage works in reverse — 2025: revenue up 6.1 percent, profit up 23.4 percent (4,232 to 5,221 M€). That is the operating leverage [business cycles](/kurser/km-057-konjunkturcykler) make intelligible — in both directions.

## Customer prepayments — the customer's capital builds the aircraft

At contract signing the airline pays an advance; further payments follow production milestones. Customer prepayments are formally a liability — but also capital that gets to finance production: the customer finances its own aircraft while it is being built. Airbus's balance sheet carries the mechanics: cash of 13.1 billion euro against 14.3 billion in traditional interest-bearing debt, debt-to-equity 0.55 — fundamentally balanced despite thousands of aircraft in the pipeline.

Two warnings. First: prepayments are earned funds, not yet revenue — they unwind as deliveries are recognized, so the debt picture moves with the order book. Second: aviation balance sheets are full of leasing — much of the world's fleet is owned by leasing companies, not airlines, making the interest rate the sector's hidden cycle engine: a higher rate makes fleet renewal dearer, the order book slower. Balance sheet building blocks: [the balance sheet in 15 minutes](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-balansrakning-pa-15-minuter); lease accounting: [Leasing](/kurser/km-023-leasing); interest pricing: [Interest — the price of money](/kurser/km-054-ranta).

## The engine aftermarket — the moat after delivery

Razor and blades: the razor sells cheap, the profit lives on the blades for decades. The engine maker earns on service, overhauls and spare parts as long as the engine flies — typically two to three decades. Every engine leaving the factory is a future service stream, and the installed base grows with every delivery. It is a [moat](/kurser/mt-01-vad-ar-en-moat) of the most durable kind: installed engines are not replaced because a competitor launches a new one — the [moat test](/kurser/mt-02-moat-erosion-och-vallgravstest) is about the service share, not new orders.

The universe's numbers carry the mechanics. GE Aerospace gross margin 31.1 percent against Airbus 16.3 — nearly double; ROIC 27.5 against 20.5; EBIT margin 20.6 against 8.7. ROIC there despite the development costs of an engine program shows the aftermarket's quality — reading ROIC in that type of business: [ROIC — the forgotten key ratio](/blogg/roic-den-glomda-nyckeltalen-v11). The airframe half holds the same structure, weaker: service and spare parts on delivered aircraft give recurring revenue, but the core delivery is series manufacturing — margins of another life than software's. Keeping cash flow positive through a cyclical swing is the airframe half's achievement: Airbus's free cash flow was positive all four years, 3,824 → 3,204 → 3,733 → 4,031 M€ 2022–2025, FCF margin 6.1 percent. The full cash flow analysis: [Cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen); margin comparisons across business models: [gross margin analysis](/blogg/v07-bruttomarginal-analys).

## Multiple and cycle — how to read the valuation

Multiples for the halves: Airbus at P/E 25.9 (forward 24.4) and EV/EBIT 22.0; GE Aerospace at P/E 39.0 and EV/EBIT 33.8 — against the universe's industrials median: P/E 26.9 and EV/EBIT 21.8, same data (14 companies). The difference is structure, not mood: GE's multiple carries the aftermarket's higher margins and consensus EPS growth of +14.7 percent next year; Airbus's forward multiple reflects around +6.5 percent. Both PEG ratios sit high (4.0 and 4.2 on one-year forecasts) — PEG has documented weaknesses: [the weaknesses of the PEG multiple](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026). Basic multiple reading: [the P/E ratio](/kurser/km-009-pe) and [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit).

P/B — 5.9 for Airbus against 19.4 for GE — says most about how little booked machinery value the carrying value rests on: installed base and order book are assets the balance sheet only skims. The cycle: aircraft are ordered in good times, delivered years later — the sector's cycle is long, deliveries lag; order intake is the leading signal, deliveries the confirmation. [The industrials sector](/kurser/km-041-industrisektorn) is the natural neighbor — both aviation halves sit there.

## How to read the report — five points

- **Delivery count.** Aircraft per quarter and year — revenue's engine, the year's sales driver.
- **Order intake and order book.** Count and value; intake above deliveries (book-to-bill above 1) grows the buffer.
- **Customer prepayments on the balance sheet.** Do they move with the order book? A falling prepayment balance on stagnant intake is worth understanding.
- **Aftermarket share and segments.** How much of revenue is service and spare parts — and at what margins?
- **Program costs and one-offs.** Space programs, restructurings, legal processes — check how much of profit is adjusted, the discipline of [Cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen).

## The summary

- Aerospace stocks mean the manufacturing side: Airbus the airframe, GE Aerospace the engines — not the airlines that fly.
- The order book is the earnings buffer: here 8,000 ÷ 800 = ten years of production sold — but Airbus 2023 (revenue +11.4, profit −10.8 percent) shows inflation eating the margin despite a full book.
- Prepayments finance the pipeline: cash 13.1 against debt 14.3 billion euro, debt-to-equity 0.55.
- The aftermarket is the moat: GE gross margin 31.1 against Airbus 16.3 percent, ROIC 27.5 percent — installations earn for decades.
- The multiple difference is structural: P/E 25.9 against 39.0, but both PEG ratios above 4 — forecast risk is the price of the buffer.

Continuation: [The aviation sector](/kurser/se-10-flyg) in course form; [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) for context.
